source_material.exact_excerpt: The length of a syllable must be distinguished from that of a vowel.

records.editorial_analysis: Cook distinguishes a long vowel from a syllable made heavy by following consonants. His terms long by nature and long by position should be translated into clear vowel-length versus syllable-weight language.
limits: A short vowel does not become long simply because its syllable is heavy.
This section is not evidence for any new macron on a course word.

candidate_examples.comment: Use with SH-CK-47: word is a heavy syllable with a short vowel; hof has the short-stem plural hofu.

records.editorial_analysis: Useful terminology background for distinguishing a consonant becoming palatal from the separate influence of an already palatal consonant on a following vowel.
limits: Cook’s printed-vowel palatal rules are too broad to turn into an exceptionless pronunciation algorithm; Fulk and the accepted pronunciation convention should control historical qualifications.
Do not import Cook’s modern-English pronunciation approximations as a revision to the accepted pronunciation guide.

source_material.exact_excerpt: The cause of i-umlaut was in all cases an i or a j (pronounced like Mod. Eng. y) of a following syllable
source_material.following_sentence_summary: The conditioning i/j usually disappeared before historic Old English or became e.
source_material.exact_qualification: Strictly speaking, i is not the umlaut of e, but the phenomenon, though resulting from a somewhat different cause, is virtually the same.

records.editorial_analysis: The visible root alternation may survive after its historical trigger has disappeared. This explains why learners cannot apply a present-day final-letter rule. The ordinary teaching umbrella includes alternations with different chronological histories.
limits: Do not present the entire printed table as one simultaneous sound change: Cook himself separates e→i in strict historical terms.
Fulk’s historical treatment is needed to distinguish older raising from later mutation for the e/ēo presents.
Cook notes that apparent gold/gylden o→y depends on earlier u, so modern-looking vowel correspondences alone do not prove the historical input.
For unfamiliar nasal-letter comparisons, preserve Cook’s ǫ rather than silently changing it to o or a.

candidate_examples.use: Derivational ō/ē comparison, with a supplied semantic gloss.
Present ū/ȳ comparison.
ea/ie comparison and link to later y/i spellings.
Useful contrast with ablaut, explicitly label the older historical raising qualification.
Visible eo/ie contrast; source labels it umlaut.

source_material.source_claim: Initial g, c, sc affect front vowels; sc also has additional listed back-vowel effects.

records.editorial_analysis: This is the vowel effect following palatal consonants, normally called palatal diphthongization. It is conceptually distinct from palatalization of the consonant itself.
limits: Cook prints input/output pairs without asterisks; do not thereby certify all printed inputs as historically attested forms in the intended dialect.
Do not treat every c/g before an e/i spelling as palatal solely from this section.
The additional sc patterns need Fulk’s treatment and dialect/chronology qualification before learner use.

candidate_examples.use: Familiar outcomes; preserve short ea versus long ēa.

source_material.exact_excerpt: Remember that y or i, short or long, may stand for ie, short or long.

records.editorial_analysis: A useful practical link between historical explanation, dialect/date variation and dictionary lookup: the same y spelling need not always go back to original u.
limits: Do not equate these variants indiscriminately in all words or silently replace source spellings.
Cook’s note identifies possible correspondences, not complete dating or dialect distribution.

candidate_examples.use: A labelled spelling/word-history example, not permission to swap letters in any entry.

source_material.source_rule: A u or o in the following syllable may change a to ea, e/i to eo, and sometimes i to io.
source_material.exact_qualification: The change of vowel is, however, not invariable in these circumstances, and, on the whole, may be regarded as exceptional.

records.editorial_analysis: Contrast the following-vowel cause with the following-consonant cause of breaking. Cook explicitly recognizes that back mutation is not automatic.
limits: Use Fulk for the dialect-specific consonant environments and distribution.
Cook’s illustrative articulatory kæuru-like intermediate (printed as cæuru) is an explanatory approximation, not a newly attested OE word.

candidate_examples.use: A bounded variant pair if glossary support is supplied.
Combine only with the separately recorded w-effect in SH-CK-26; no automatic inverse rule.

source_material.source_rule: Before r + consonant, l + consonant, and h + consonant or final h, a is regularly converted into ea, and e or i frequently into eo.
source_material.exact_qualification: strictly speaking, when we say that a was broken, we should rather say that it was æ

records.editorial_analysis: Cook explains a glide arising between a front vowel and a following back articulation. His rule is an aggregate description: it does not assert that all listed vowels break identically in every environment.
limits: Write the actual short-vowel input as æ rather than treating a→ea as the immediate change.
Fulk supplies the finer restrictions, especially æ versus e before l + consonant; retain those before drafting.
Cook’s historical input forms are printed without reconstruction stars. Any selected earlier stage needs explicit status and should not become an unqualified course vocabulary entry.
His drawled Shakespeare/Modern-English analogies are optional historical explanation, not the course pronunciation norm.
Do not explain every written ea/eo by breaking: palatal influence and back mutation are separate causes.

candidate_examples.use: æ-breaking outcomes; label the word sense, especially earm noun versus adjective.
e-breaking outcomes with the appropriate consonant environment.

source_material.exact_excerpt: Ablaut is not to be confounded with umlaut.

records.editorial_analysis: Ablaut is the inherited stem-vowel relationship behind strong-verb principal parts. Umlaut is historically conditioned by a following sound. The English sing/sang/sung comparison is a useful familiar entry point.
limits: Cook’s statement that ablaut must simply be accepted is a pedagogical boundary, not a claim that modern historical linguistics offers no deeper explanation.
Do not represent all strong-verb principal-part vowels as unchanged Indo-European vowels; later OE changes have affected them.

candidate_examples.use: Image-checked full principal parts in SH-CK-104 allow comparison with hilpð; distinguish ablaut from later breaking and older present raising.

source_material.source_rule: An unstressed internal vowel may be reduced or lost, with syncope most likely after a long syllable.

records.editorial_analysis: Explain why endings can expose different stem shapes without turning a lexical tendency into a universal deletion rule.
limits: The noun-specific refinements and attested retained vowels at §43.4, pp28–29, must accompany practical applications.
A heavy syllable does not mean that its vowel is long.

candidate_examples.use: Compact familiar example of internal vowel loss.

records.topic: Nasal spelling and effects of w

source_material.exact_qualification: When o, u, or y immediately follows w, it may be suspected, though it must not be assumed, that the vowel was once eo or io

records.editorial_analysis: Useful small notes showing that sound histories may interact and that dictionary lookup must allow documented variants.
limits: Do not infer a reconstructed chain solely from a word’s modern-looking spelling.
Keep the marked nasal vowel ǫ distinct in exact source transcription.

records.topic: Loss, vocalization, contraction and compensatory lengthening
records.editorial_analysis: Final consonants may reappear before endings, or an intervocalic consonant may be lost with a changed vowel. Use a small number of named lexical examples.
limits: The actual Cook spelling in §29 is gefeon without a printed macron; do not silently turn that exact citation into gefēon. A normalized headword needs its own declared evidence.
The separate g-loss and h-loss environments are not interchangeable.
The actual source includes lexical qualifiers such as certain words, often and frequently.

candidate_examples.use: Familiar contraction/length example, corroborated by §47.5 p33.
Optional w-alternation example if useful.

records.editorial_analysis: Optional short reference notes: loss of a nasal before a fricative with compensatory vowel lengthening; transposition of sounds in metathesis.
limits: Cook’s unstarred historical input forms are not automatically attested Old English.
Do not reconstruct ancestral spellings beyond the evidence merely to add a historical chain.
The source has long ā in the asking variants; the appendix must not silently mix these with a differently normalized course headword.

candidate_examples.use: Possible outcomes of nasal loss, with the reconstructed stages omitted or explicitly labelled.

records.editorial_analysis: Consonant changes explain opaque-looking second/third singulars and double consonants. Distinguish consonant length from vowel length, and distinguish historical j-gemination from simplification in a later cluster or at a word end.
limits: Cook’s saljan/sagjan/hrugjo- are explicitly labelled original forms, not safe unmarked OE examples.
Do not generalize every double consonant as proof of original j: Cook says many words, then gives a narrower claim for cg.
Keep assimilation intermediate forms labelled analytical or historical, not ordinary accepted answer forms.

candidate_examples.use: Familiar visible cluster changes, with productive paradigm references.
Optional j-gemination outcomes; j-stage notation only if independently approved.

records.editorial_analysis: The s/r and ð/d alternations are distinct from both vowel ablaut and ordinary spelling interchange. A short grammatical alternation note would help explain principal parts.
limits: Cook names the phenomenon but does not explain Verner’s Law here; use Fulk if that historical account is included.
Do not imply that s and r or ð and d can be freely exchanged in ordinary spelling.

candidate_examples.use: Directly image-verified s/r illustration.
Directly image-verified ð/d illustration.

records.topic: dæg/dagas, h-loss and lexical syncope limits
records.editorial_analysis: The paradigm alternation dæg/dagas is exact and familiar; a-restoration and fronting as its historical explanation require Fulk. Syncope depends on the first and second syllables and has lexical/date variation.
limits: Cook §43.2 states the visible plural alternation, not a full chronological theory of Anglo-Frisian fronting and restoration.
His syncope examples explicitly preserve exceptions and text-date effects.

candidate_examples.use: Exact paradigm comparison, with historical interpretation sourced separately to Fulk.

records.topic: Umlaut noun forms and final-vowel/weight patterns
records.editorial_analysis: Provides exact fōt/fēt and short-versus-heavy neuter patterns. The loss of final high vowels can be discussed as a historical explanation of the already taught contrast, with Fulk controlling the chronology.
limits: fēt is both the selected dative singular and nominative/accusative plural; do not label it plural only if describing the full form.
Cook records analogical and lexical variants; his -u distribution is not a universal rule for all nouns or all periods.
Do not present syncope in wæter as an absolute historical or productive rule: the page expressly preserves wæteres.

candidate_examples.use: Clear long-vowel umlaut comparison.
Syllable-weight background for final-u behavior.

records.topic: helpan principal parts and present raising

source_material.exact_qualification: A similar change, though not due to precisely the same cause (17), is found in presents in e, which is converted to i or ie

records.editorial_analysis: The four actually printed helpan principal parts permit a worked contrast with helpan/hilpð. The latter is a present alternation; it is not the mechanism creating the preterite healp.
limits: Cook’s Table104 combines inherited vowel grades with later conditioned developments; do not describe healp’s ea as an untouched original ablaut vowel.
Preserve quantity: these classIII vowels/diphthongs are explicitly all short.

candidate_examples.use: Best single worked contrast for ablaut, breaking and older present raising.

records.topic: Comparative evidence for lost i/j triggers

source_material.title: I-UMLAUT ILLUSTRATED FROM GOTHIC
source_material.exact_excerpt: it would be a serious error to regard Gothic as the parent of the other Germanic tongues

records.editorial_analysis: The retained j/i in cognate Gothic endings makes the missing conditioning element intelligible. A single clearly labelled comparison may be more useful than an invented reconstruction chain.
limits: Gothic forms are comparisons, not ancestral Old English or new OE glossary entries.
The Bible quotations are not an assigned reading or exercise.
Cook’s claim about Gothic’s overall antiquity need not be copied into the learner appendix.

candidate_examples.use: Optional one-line comparative evidence, explicitly not a parent-to-child derivation.

source_fidelity: Original printed forms are preserved separately from editorial interpretation and candidate learner uses.
Cook frequently prints historical input forms without asterisks. Their presence is not a claim of OE textual attestation; any reconstructed learner form requires explicit labelling.
Cook’s hooked e/marked nasal o are transcribed as ę/ǫ; macrons are retained on the first element of diphthongs.
No changes to course spelling, paradigms, glossary entries, teaching milestones or exercise assignments are authorized by this audit.
Candidate glossary routes are exact-data matches only; empty routes require coordinator disposition, not automatic new headwords.
recommended_core: Notation, vowel quantity versus syllable weight, and historically conditioned changes
Breaking with vowel-specific conditions supplied by Fulk
Ablaut versus present raising, using helpan/healp/hilpð
A short selection of gemination, assimilation, contraction and grammatical consonant alternation

reconciliation_points.need: Fulk must narrow the aggregate §21 l+C rule by input vowel and clarify any rj exception.
Keep older e→i separate historically from i-umlaut; Fulk supplies the ēo→īe intermediate analysis.
Cook’s dæg/dagas is directly verified, but the historical explanation is not given by §43.2; cite Fulk for it.
No treatment under that term was located in Cook’s early §§12–37; this topic needs Fulk evidence rather than an invented Cook locator.
Cook gives useful visible weight-dependent -u patterns; chronological historical explanation requires Fulk.
Cook §37 provides exact grammatical consonant alternations, not their full historical explanation.
